summary: Cetilistat is a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor used as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie, low-fat diet for the management of obesity. It acts locally in the gut to inhibit pancreatic and gastric lipases, reducing the hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides and thereby decreasing fat absorption, with the unabsorbed fat passed in the stool. The usual dose is 120 mg three times daily with or just after each main fat-containing meal. Because the mechanism is similar to orlistat, the main adverse effects are gastrointestinal and fat-related (oily stools, faecal urgency, flatus with discharge), and long-term use may reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Cetilistat is approved in Japan and some other countries but is NOT approved by the US FDA; dosing here is based on manufacturer/SmPC-type sources and published data.

moa: Cetilistat is a potent inhibitor of gastrointestinal lipases (pancreatic and gastric). It binds the active serine site of these enzymes in the gut lumen, preventing them from hydrolysing dietary triglycerides into absorbable free fatty acids and monoglycerides. The undigested fat is not absorbed and is eliminated in the faeces, producing a modest reduction in caloric intake and supporting weight loss when combined with a low-fat, reduced-calorie diet. Systemic absorption of cetilistat is minimal, so its action is essentially local.

relative: Concomitant drugs whose absorption may be reduced (e.g. some fat-soluble vitamins, ciclosporin, levothyroxine, anticonvulsants)
monitor: Fat-soluble vitamin status on prolonged use
Glycaemic and lipid control where relevant

preg: Cetilistat is not recommended during pregnancy. Weight-loss therapy is generally inappropriate in pregnancy, and there are insufficient data on use of cetilistat in pregnant women.
lact: It is not recommended during breastfeeding because of insufficient safety data; the potential reduction in maternal fat-soluble vitamin absorption is also a consideration.
renal: Cetilistat acts within the gastrointestinal tract with minimal systemic absorption, so renal impairment is not expected to materially alter its action; no specific dose adjustment has been established, and it should be used with general caution.
hepatic: There are limited data in hepatic impairment; cetilistat is contraindicated in cholestasis. Use with caution in other liver disease and monitor for tolerability.

major: May reduce absorption of ciclosporin - separate dosing and monitor ciclosporin levels

pearls: NOT FDA-approved - approved in Japan and some other markets; information based on manufacturer/SmPC-type sources and published data, mechanism analogous to orlistat
Acts locally in the gut with minimal systemic absorption - main effects are gastrointestinal and fat-related
Reducing dietary fat reduces both the side effects and is required for efficacy
Long-term use can impair absorption of fat-soluble vitamins - supplement separately if needed
Omit the dose with fat-free or missed meals
missed: If you miss a dose with a meal, do not take it later; just take the next dose with your next main fat-containing meal. There is no benefit to taking a dose without food.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited. Because systemic absorption is minimal, significant systemic toxicity is unlikely; excess doses would mainly increase gastrointestinal adverse effects. Manage supportively and observe.
